### KV cache in distributed settings {#sec-inference-scale-kv-cache-distributed-settings-712e}

Routing a request to a shard group, or moving a conversation to a different group, decides where its KV state lives. The sharding strategies of @sec-inference-scale-model-sharding-inference-82b3 fix that placement inside a group. Pipeline parallelism keeps each layer's cache on the stage that owns that layer, so tensor parallelism is the case that reshapes cache management, and migration is the case that moves it between groups.

Under tensor parallelism, the KV cache is sharded\index{KV Cache!tensor parallel sharding} across devices along with attention heads. Each device stores cache for its subset of heads. A multi-head attention layout spreads many KV heads across the group, while grouped-query attention with eight KV heads leaves one per device in an eight-way group.

```
8-way tensor parallelism, 64 KV heads (MHA):
Device 0: KV cache for heads 0-7
Device 1: KV cache for heads 8-15
...
Device 7: KV cache for heads 56-63
```

Cross-device sharing adds a constraint. Prefix caching across tensor-parallel devices requires cache to be sharded identically on all devices. This is automatic when prefixes are processed with the same tensor-parallel configuration.

KV cache migration\index{KV Cache!migration} presents a further challenge. When the router moves a conversation to a different replica because of failure or rebalancing (routing keyed on a hash of the session ID, the consistent-hashing scheme developed in @sec-inference-scale-consistent-hashing-stateful-routing-ae5b), the service must either transfer available KV state or rebuild it. Transfer requires a reachable source or a saved copy; after an unrecoverable replica failure, the service rebuilds from authoritative conversation history:

```
Migration options:
1. Rebuild: Re-run prefill on new replica (cost grows with context length)
2. Transfer: Send KV cache over network (cache bytes / link bandwidth)
3. Hybrid: Transfer if small, rebuild if large

Decision threshold:
if cache_size_bytes/network_bandwidth < prefill_time:
    transfer()
else:
    rebuild()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: kv-migration-cost
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ KV CACHE MIGRATION: TRANSFER VS REBUILD (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: KV cache migration paragraph in the sharded-routing section.
# │
# │ Goal: Compare shipping a 4K-context KV cache over 100 GbE with rebuilding it
# │       by prefill on an eight-GPU tensor-parallel group.
# │ Show: ~1.3 GB cache, ~168 MB per device, ~13 ms shard transfer, ~107 ms
# │       full transfer, ~5.8e14 FLOP prefill, ~180 ms rebuild.
# │ How: Llama3_70B.get_kv_cache_size (GQA); Systems.Fabrics.Ethernet_100G;
# │      prefill FLOPs = 2 x params x tokens at the batched-inference MFU anchor.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_int, fmt_math, fmt_memory, fmt_percent, fmt_time, sci_latex

class KvMigrationCost:
    """Transfer-versus-rebuild cost for migrating one conversation's KV cache."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    context_tokens = int(ReferenceStats.ServingProfiles.PrecisionDividendContextLengthTokens)
    tp_degree = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100.accelerators_per_node
    link_bw = Systems.Fabrics.Ethernet_100G.bandwidth
    gpu_peak = Hardware.Cloud.H100.compute.peak_flops
    prefill_mfu = Literature.Training.MfuInferenceBatched

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    kv_total = model.get_kv_cache_size(context_tokens, 1)
    kv_per_device = kv_total / tp_degree
    shard_transfer = (kv_per_device / link_bw).to(ms)
    full_transfer = (kv_total / link_bw).to(ms)
    params = model.parameters.to(param).magnitude
    prefill_flops = 2 * params * context_tokens
    rebuild_time = (prefill_flops * flop / (tp_degree * gpu_peak * prefill_mfu)).to(ms)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(shard_transfer * 5 < rebuild_time, "Parallel shard transfer should win clearly")
    check(full_transfer < rebuild_time < 3 * full_transfer, "Single-link full transfer should still win, but by a smaller margin")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    kv_total_gb_str = fmt_memory(kv_total, unit=GB, precision=1, commas=False)
    kv_per_device_mb_str = fmt_memory(round(kv_per_device.to(MB).magnitude) * MB, unit=MB, precision=0, commas=False)
    tp_degree_str = fmt_int(tp_degree, commas=False)
    link_bw_gbps_str = fmt_bandwidth(link_bw, unit=Gbps, precision=0, commas=False)
    link_bw_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(link_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=1, commas=False)
    shard_transfer_ms_str = fmt_time(round(shard_transfer.magnitude) * ms, ms, precision=0, commas=False)
    full_transfer_ms_str = fmt_time(round(full_transfer.magnitude) * ms, ms, precision=0, commas=False)
    rebuild_ms_str = fmt_time(round(rebuild_time.magnitude, -1) * ms, ms, precision=0, commas=False)
    prefill_mfu_pct_str = fmt_percent(prefill_mfu, precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
    context_tokens_str = fmt_int(context_tokens, commas=True)
    prefill_flops_math = fmt_math(rf"{sci_latex(prefill_flops, precision=1)}")
    prefill_operands_math = fmt_math(rf"2 \times {sci_latex(params, precision=1)}")
```

For Llama 3 70B with GQA and a `{python} KvMigrationCost.context_tokens_str`-token context, KV cache is about `{python} KvMigrationCost.kv_total_gb_str` total per sequence, or about `{python} KvMigrationCost.kv_per_device_mb_str` per device under `{python} KvMigrationCost.tp_degree_str`-way tensor parallelism. At `{python} KvMigrationCost.link_bw_gbps_str` (`{python} KvMigrationCost.link_bw_gb_per_s_str`), transferring one shard takes roughly `{python} KvMigrationCost.shard_transfer_ms_str`, while transferring the full cache would take about `{python} KvMigrationCost.full_transfer_ms_str`. Rebuilding the same context requires about `{python} KvMigrationCost.prefill_flops_math` FLOPs of prefill (`{python} KvMigrationCost.prefill_operands_math` parameters $\times$ `{python} KvMigrationCost.context_tokens_str` tokens), roughly `{python} KvMigrationCost.rebuild_ms_str` on the same tensor-parallel group at `{python} KvMigrationCost.prefill_mfu_pct_str` utilization. Parallel shard transfer therefore wins by a substantial margin, while a single-link full-cache transfer still wins by a smaller margin. Transfer time grows linearly with context, while prefill cost grows faster once attention over the long prompt dominates, so transfer becomes decisive at long context.

The shard group boundary also defines readiness. A group can accept work only when the devices, model state, and cache capacity required for its execution plan are available, so the load balancer needs a health signal for the serving replica as a whole.

### Health checking and failover {#sec-inference-scale-health-checking-failover-070e}

Load balancers can route around failure only if the health signal\index{Health checking!failover detection} matches the failure mode. @Sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-health-checking-a604 separates liveness, readiness, and inference-correctness checks and shows how probe settings bound failover time. On an accelerator replica, each tier must test a different part of the serving state, because a process that is alive may still be unusable when its weights are not loaded, its memory pool is exhausted, or its first request will trigger a long warmup. The probes therefore escalate from cheapest to most realistic:

```
GET  /health/live       -> 200 (process alive) or timeout (process dead)
GET  /health/ready      -> 200 (weights loaded, device initialized) or 503
POST /health/inference  -> 200 with valid output for a fixed test prompt, or error
```

Only the deep inference probe detects a replica that answers liveness checks while failing on real requests, for example because its memory pool is too fragmented to admit a request or its model state never finished warming, and a strong deep probe checks the output itself, comparing logits for the fixed prompt against expected bounds. Readiness should likewise test free accelerator memory and warmup state, not process start alone. Once a replica fails these probes, the failover mechanics of @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-failover-mechanisms-5ddd take over, including reconstruction of any KV-cache state the failed replica held.

### Circuit breakers and backpressure {#sec-inference-scale-circuit-breakers-backpressure-e61c}

When a GPU inference server slows down, routing more requests to it can turn a local slowdown into a fleet-wide failure. Thermal throttling is a typical trigger: a replica that normally serves a request in 50 ms begins taking 500 ms, queues fill behind it, client timeouts generate retries, and those retries push load onto neighboring replicas. The load balancer needs a way to stop treating that replica as merely slow and start treating it as unavailable.

The circuit breaker pattern\index{Circuit Breaker!circuit breaker pattern} [@nygard2007releaseit] provides that control. In the closed state, the server receives normal traffic. When error rate, timeout rate, or latency exceeds a threshold, the breaker opens and requests fail fast or route elsewhere instead of waiting behind a saturated queue. After a recovery interval, the breaker becomes half-open: it admits a small number of probe requests, closes if they succeed, and reopens if they fail. The important systems property is bounded blast radius. The failed replica loses traffic quickly enough that its queue cannot export overload to the rest of the fleet. @Fig-circuit-breaker traces the three states and the transitions between them.

::: {#fig-circuit-breaker fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Circuit breaker states**: The circuit breaker protects the system from cascading failure. Closed: normal operation. Open: error threshold exceeded; all requests fail fast to prevent resource exhaustion. Half-open: after a timeout, a limited number of requests are allowed through to probe the dependency's health. Success resets to closed; failure returns to open." fig-alt="State diagram with three rectangular state blocks. The green closed state transitions to the red open state when failures exceed a threshold. After a timeout, open transitions to the orange half-open state, which returns to closed after a successful probe or to open after a failed probe."}
![](images/svg/circuit-breaker.svg)

:::

Backpressure propagation\index{Backpressure!propagation} complements the breaker by making overload visible upstream. When queue depth crosses a threshold, the server returns a signal such as `503 Service Unavailable`; the load balancer marks the replica as degraded and routes fewer requests to it. If all replicas become degraded, the system shifts from routing control to admission control\index{Admission Control!overload shedding}, rejecting some requests at the edge rather than accepting work it cannot serve within the latency SLO; the load-shedding policies of @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-load-shedding-8476 decide which requests to reject first. Circuit breakers isolate unhealthy replicas; backpressure tells the rest of the system to slow down before retries amplify the failure.

Backpressure works only when the request contract propagates through the whole serving graph. The gateway converts the client timeout into an absolute deadline and every downstream stage subtracts elapsed time before admitting more work. If the client disconnects or the deadline expires, cancellation must reach queued CPU work, accelerator batches, retrieval calls, and streamed output. A canceled request that remains in a continuous batch is zombie work\index{Zombie work!cancelled request drain}: it consumes KV pages and decode bandwidth while producing no useful response. Some kernels cannot be interrupted mid-launch, so cancellation commonly takes effect at the next batch or token boundary; the scheduler must measure that cancellation lag rather than promise instantaneous preemption.

The same request identifier must connect routing, queueing, prefill, decode, cache allocation, and response streaming. A useful serving trace records admitted and rejected requests, queue delay, TTFT, TPOT, input and output tokens, cache pages, batch membership, preemptions, cancellations, and fallback decisions. Aggregate accelerator utilization cannot distinguish useful work from late or canceled work. SLO goodput and wasted-token rate close that gap by reporting how much completed work met its contract and how much execution the system performed after the result had lost value.

A saturated LLM fleet operating under severe KV cache pressure has three domain-specific relief valves that generic backpressure cannot provide. First, engines can apply context eviction\index{Context eviction!KV cache pressure} by using an explicitly supported sliding-window or approximate cache-eviction policy with a quality check, or by truncating the retained history and recomputing its state. Silently dropping old KV entries is not equivalent to recomputing a shorter conversation, because later cached states already depend on the earlier context. Schedulers can also temporarily disable speculative decoding, reclaiming the GPU memory that its draft model occupies. Finally, fallback routing\index{Fallback routing!graceful degradation} redirects incoming requests to a smaller quantized fallback model until the primary queue drains, an instance of the model-fallback ladder in @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-model-fallback-bc6e.

Each response trades output quality or latency for continued availability, which is often preferable to rejection from the user's perspective. The system designer must specify which degradation modes are acceptable at each pressure tier, because the correct trade-off depends on the application. A real-time assistant, for example, tolerates context truncation better than silent quality degradation.

Efficient routing assumes that each replica's hardware serves one workload, yet critical production models often share physical clusters with experimental models and developer endpoints. Keeping a rogue query from degrading a production service then requires multi-tenant isolation.

## Multi-Tenancy and Isolation {#sec-inference-scale-multitenancy-isolation-688c}

Consider a critical customer-support chatbot running on the same GPU server as an experimental computer vision script. If the experimental workload accidentally monopolizes the PCIe bus or memory bandwidth, the customer-facing chatbot begins timing out, violating its SLO. Multi-tenancy and isolation ensure that co-located workloads save money without sacrificing the predictability of flagship services. Fleet quotas, fair-share hierarchies, and priority preemption (@sec-fleet-orchestration-multi-tenancy) decide how much of the cluster a serving system receives; the problem here is keeping the tenants who share that allocation from degrading each other, request by request.

### The multi-tenancy challenge {#sec-inference-scale-multitenancy-challenge-8dca}

Sharing a serving pool among tenants raises utilization, reduces the number of clusters to operate, and makes aggregate traffic more predictable than any one tenant's traffic, the same statistical-multiplexing gain that motivates device sharing at fleet level (@sec-fleet-orchestration-gpu-sharing).

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol2_inference_margin_004.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="A red tenant workload fans gray arrows to five blue peer workloads, showing one source degrading many shared dependents."}

*One tenant's burst can degrade every workload sharing the pool.*
:::

The cost is interference. A burst from one tenant can degrade every other tenant through shared KV-cache memory, network bandwidth, and accelerator time; tenant data must remain separated; and a pool that serves tenants with different SLOs must still honor the tightest of them. Noisy-neighbor effects come first because they are the most direct threat to a latency contract.

### Noisy neighbor problems {#sec-inference-scale-noisy-neighbor-problems-1b87}

The noisy neighbor problem\index{Multi-tenancy!noisy neighbor problem} occurs when one tenant's workload degrades performance for others sharing the same infrastructure. The interference manifests across three resource dimensions simultaneously.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: noisy-neighbor-impact
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ NOISY NEIGHBOR IMPACT (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-inference-scale-noisy-neighbor-problems-1b87 KV-pool paragraph
# │          and the quantifying-noisy-neighbor example.
# │
# │ Goal: Show how one tenant's long-context burst shrinks the other tenants'
# │       admissible batches, and what per-tenant quotas preserve.
# │ Show: 60 GB pool, 20 GB shares, 45 GB swollen share, 200 -> 75 sequences,
# │       62.5 percent reduction; 100 -> 500 QPS burst under a 50 ms SLO.
# │ How: Equal static shares; the swollen tenant's excess is taken evenly from
# │      the other two. All inputs are scenario assumptions.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_rate, fmt_time

class NoisyNeighborImpact:
    """KV-pool contention and quota protection for a shared serving pool."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    kv_pool = 60 * GB  # scenario assumption: shared KV-cache pool
    pool_tenants = 3  # scenario assumption: tenants sharing that pool
    swollen_share = 45 * GB  # scenario assumption: long-context tenant's share
    base_seqs = 200  # scenario assumption: sequences per equal share
    tenant_base_qps = 100  # scenario assumption: per-tenant request rate
    tenant_burst_qps = 500  # scenario assumption: bursting tenant's rate
    slo_ms = 50  # scenario assumption: P99 SLO
    p99_low_ms = 22  # scenario assumption: unprotected pool P99, low end
    p99_high_ms = 45  # scenario assumption: unprotected pool P99, high end
    throttled_qps = 120  # scenario assumption: quota-enforced rate
    protected_p99_ms = 15  # scenario assumption: protected tenants' P99

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    base_share = kv_pool / pool_tenants
    gb_per_seq = base_share / base_seqs
    other_share = (kv_pool - swollen_share) / (pool_tenants - 1)
    other_seqs = int((other_share / gb_per_seq).to("").magnitude)
    batch_reduction = 1 - other_seqs / base_seqs
    burst_mult = tenant_burst_qps / tenant_base_qps

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(other_seqs < base_seqs, "The burst must shrink the other tenants' batches")
    check(p99_high_ms < slo_ms, "Unprotected P99 in this scenario stays below the SLO")
    check(protected_p99_ms < p99_low_ms, "Quotas must protect the other tenants' latency")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    kv_pool_gb_str = fmt_memory(kv_pool, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    base_share_gb_str = fmt_memory(base_share, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    swollen_share_gb_str = fmt_memory(swollen_share, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    base_seqs_str = fmt_int(base_seqs, commas=False)
    other_seqs_str = fmt_int(other_seqs, commas=False)
    batch_reduction_pct_str = fmt_percent(batch_reduction, precision=1, commas=False, style="prose")
    tenant_base_qps_str = fmt_rate(tenant_base_qps, "QPS")
    tenant_burst_qps_str = fmt_rate(tenant_burst_qps, "QPS")
    burst_mult_str = fmt_multiple(burst_mult, precision=0, commas=False)
    slo_ms_str = fmt_time(slo_ms * millisecond, millisecond, precision=0, commas=False)
    p99_low_ms_str = fmt_time(p99_low_ms * millisecond, millisecond, precision=0, commas=False)
    p99_high_ms_str = fmt_time(p99_high_ms * millisecond, millisecond, precision=0, commas=False)
    tenant_throttled_qps_str = fmt_rate(throttled_qps, "QPS")
    protected_p99_ms_str = fmt_time(protected_p99_ms * millisecond, millisecond, precision=0, commas=False)
```

GPU memory contention\index{Resource contention!GPU memory} is the most severe: a tenant with unexpectedly long sequences can consume a disproportionate share of the KV cache pool. Consider three tenants sharing a `{python} NoisyNeighborImpact.kv_pool_gb_str` KV cache pool with equal `{python} NoisyNeighborImpact.base_share_gb_str` allocations. When one tenant begins issuing long-context requests, its allocation can swell to `{python} NoisyNeighborImpact.swollen_share_gb_str`, forcing evictions that reduce the other tenants from `{python} NoisyNeighborImpact.base_seqs_str` concurrent sequences each to `{python} NoisyNeighborImpact.other_seqs_str`, a `{python} NoisyNeighborImpact.batch_reduction_pct_str` batch-size reduction that directly degrades their throughput. Egress bandwidth and accelerator time-sharing add the device-level interference channels of @sec-fleet-orchestration-resource-isolation, so a noisy-neighbor measurement must capture all three dimensions at once.

::: {#exmp-inference-quantifying-noisy-neighbor-impact .callout-example title="Quantifying noisy neighbor impact"}

**Scenario**: An inference platform serves 10 tenants on shared H100 GPUs at `{python} NoisyNeighborImpact.tenant_base_qps_str` each under a `{python} NoisyNeighborImpact.slo_ms_str` P99 SLO. Tenant 3 bursts to `{python} NoisyNeighborImpact.tenant_burst_qps_str`, `{python} NoisyNeighborImpact.burst_mult_str` its baseline.

**Diagnosis**: Without isolation, KV cache and compute contention raise P99 latency across the whole pool into the `{python} NoisyNeighborImpact.p99_low_ms_str` to `{python} NoisyNeighborImpact.p99_high_ms_str` range. The SLO still holds, but every tenant has lost much of its headroom. With per-tenant quotas enabled, enforcement throttles Tenant 3 to `{python} NoisyNeighborImpact.tenant_throttled_qps_str`, violating only Tenant 3's SLO, while the other nine tenants keep their normal `{python} NoisyNeighborImpact.protected_p99_ms_str` P99.

**Systems lesson**: Shared capacity raises utilization only when it is coupled with isolation. Quotas turn pool-wide erosion of latency headroom into an admission decision confined to the tenant that caused it; without them, a larger burst or a tighter SLO turns the same erosion into violations across the pool.

:::

### Resource quotas and fair sharing {#sec-inference-scale-resource-quotas-fair-sharing-006c}

Resource quotas\index{Resource quota!fair sharing} limit what each tenant can consume, preventing any single tenant from monopolizing shared resources. Hard quotas turn shared serving into admission control. Request rate and concurrency bound arrival pressure, while input tokens, output tokens, KV-cache pages, accelerator time, and egress bytes bound the work performed after admission. A single scalar quota cannot protect all of these resources because two requests can have the same count but differ by orders of magnitude in prompt length or generated output. @Lst-resource-quotas shows representative gates so a tenant can be throttled at the scarce resource boundary instead of degrading the whole batch.

::: {#lst-resource-quotas lst-cap="**Multidimensional Resource Quotas**: A snapshot check compares prospective resource use with tenant limits. Atomic reservation and scheduler enforcement are separate requirements."}

```{.python}
class TenantQuota:
    max_concurrent_requests: int  # e.g., 100
    max_kv_cache_mb: int  # e.g., 20,000
    max_qps: int  # e.g., 1,000
    max_input_tokens_per_minute: int
    max_output_tokens_per_minute: int
    max_batch_tokens: int  # e.g., 50,000


def check_quota_snapshot(tenant_id, request):
    quota = get_quota(tenant_id)
    usage = get_usage(tenant_id)

    if usage.concurrent + 1 > quota.max_concurrent_requests:
        return RateLimitError("concurrent request limit")
    if usage.kv_cache_mb + request.reserved_kv_mb > quota.max_kv_cache_mb:
        return RateLimitError("memory limit")
    if usage.requests_last_second + 1 > quota.max_qps:
        return RateLimitError("rate limit")
    if usage.input_tokens + request.input_tokens > quota.max_input_tokens_per_minute:
        return RateLimitError("input-token limit")
    if usage.output_tokens + request.max_output_tokens > quota.max_output_tokens_per_minute:
        return RateLimitError("output-token limit")

    if request.prefill_chunk_tokens > quota.max_batch_tokens:
        return RateLimitError("prefill chunk exceeds batch-token limit")

    return None  # Snapshot is eligible; no resources have been reserved.
```

:::

This listing assumes that `reserved_kv_mb` includes the requested prompt and output-token budget, and that usage counters include outstanding reservations in their stated time windows. A passing snapshot is not an admission guarantee: simultaneous callers can observe the same free capacity. Production admission must check and reserve resources atomically, roll back failed admissions, and release reservations on completion or cancellation. The batch scheduler separately enforces the aggregate batch-token limit. Quotas protect the resources they account for; shared compute, networking, and control-plane contention still require isolation and measurement.

Soft quotas relax these limits with the same guarantee-versus-maximum logic that governs fleet quotas (@sec-fleet-orchestration-burst-capacity): a tenant may burst above its nominal token rate while the pool has slack and is held to that rate when the pool saturates. What changes inside a serving system is the unit of account. Equal request counts are not equal load, because a tenant issuing long-context summarization requests consumes far more prefill compute and KV capacity than one issuing short classification queries. Token rates are better units, but input and output tokens must remain separate because they stress different phases, and memory reservation and concurrency require their own limits. With those units, the progressive-filling logic of dominant-resource fairness (@sec-fleet-orchestration-drf-worked-allocation) reduces to max-min fairness\index{Max-min fairness!token allocation} on each pool. For three tenants with output demands of 30,000, 20,000, and 80,000 tokens/sec competing for a decode pool capable of 100,000 tokens/sec, max-min fairness yields allocations of 30,000, 20,000, and 50,000. That allocation protects decode bandwidth; a separate input-token budget protects the prefill pool.

### Priority scheduling {#sec-inference-scale-priority-scheduling-3e37}

When tenants have different SLO requirements, priority scheduling\index{Priority scheduling!multi-tenant isolation} ensures that high-priority requests receive resources first. Fleet priority classes (@sec-fleet-orchestration-burst-capacity) already decide which workloads may preempt serving capacity; request priority operates inside one serving allocation, at token granularity. @Tbl-priority-scheduling-classes shows that preemption rights and resource guarantees move together down the three classes: critical traffic both preempts any lower class and reserves capacity, while best-effort never preempts and gets no guarantee, so an SLO tier maps directly onto a position in the preemption ladder.

| **Class**       |    **Use Case**    |      **Preemption**     | **Resource Guarantee** |
|:----------------|:------------------:|:-----------------------:|:----------------------:|
| **Critical**    | Revenue-generating |    Can preempt lower    |     100% reserved      |
| **Standard**    |  General traffic   | Can preempt best-effort |     Weighted share     |
| **Best-effort** | Background, batch  |      Cannot preempt     |      No guarantee      |

: **Priority scheduling classes**: Three-tier priority hierarchy for multi-tenant inference. Critical traffic gets 100 percent reserved capacity and can preempt any lower class; standard traffic shares capacity proportionally and can preempt best-effort; best-effort runs on leftover capacity with no guarantees. {#tbl-priority-scheduling-classes}

The scheduler sorts incoming requests by priority class, then by arrival time within each class. When a new critical request arrives, it jumps ahead of all standard and best-effort requests in the queue, so revenue-generating traffic does not queue behind background batch jobs, although work already running on the accelerator can still delay it.

Preemption extends this principle to requests already in flight, but priority does not make state movement free. At a token boundary, the scheduler may stop issuing decode work to a lower-priority request while retaining its KV pages, swap those pages to host memory, discard them for later recomputation, or reject the request if its deadline can no longer be met. Retention works when HBM rather than compute is plentiful; swapping works only when transfer time fits the deadline and does not congest other traffic; recomputation works when repeated prefill costs less than migration. The victim policy must account for remaining service time, state size, and deadline slack, or aggressive preemption can consume more capacity than it releases.

### Bulkhead pattern {#sec-inference-scale-bulkhead-pattern-1c3a}

The bulkhead pattern[^fn-bulkhead-service-isolation] [@nygard2007releaseit] physically isolates tenant workloads, preventing failures from propagating across tenants. The pattern is named after ship compartments that contain flooding to isolated sections.

[^fn-bulkhead-service-isolation]: [offset=-30mm] **Bulkhead limits**\index{Bulkhead Pattern!isolation}: A divider isolates failure only if it closes the relevant boundary. The Titanic's incomplete bulkheads allowed water to cascade between compartments; similarly, a soft quota cannot isolate shared memory or bandwidth that remains globally exhaustible.

The strongest form of bulkhead dedicates entire replicas to specific tenants or tenant groups. @Fig-bulkhead-patterns illustrates this deployment-level isolation between gold and standard tiers:

::: {#fig-bulkhead-patterns fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Bulkhead isolation patterns**: To prevent cascading failures in multi-tenant systems, bulkheads isolate resources. Deployment-level bulkheads (shown) assign dedicated physical replicas to high-priority tenants, separating their compute and memory pools. Request-level bulkheads enforce strict concurrency limits within shared processes. Shared networking, storage, and control-plane dependencies remain possible paths for interference." fig-alt="Two-tier system diagram. Gold tier at top with dedicated load balancer and 2 replicas. Standard tier below with shared load balancer and 3 replicas, one showing failure. Dashed line separates the tiers' dedicated serving resources."}

:::

Deployment-level bulkheads isolate the named compute and memory resources for premium tenants. They do not remove shared network, storage, power, or control-plane failure domains. The trade-off is lower pooling efficiency and additional operational overhead from dedicated infrastructure.

Request-level bulkheads complement this physical separation by limiting what any single request can consume within a shared process. Capping input length (for example, 8,000 tokens), output length (2,000 tokens), and execution time (30 seconds) prevents a single pathological request from monopolizing a GPU for minutes while other requests queue behind it.

The same boundaries confine failures. A malformed request that crashes a worker takes down only its own bulkhead, and in practice those boundaries align with service tiers.

::: {#exmp-inference-bulkhead-configuration-api-tiers .callout-example title="Bulkhead configuration for API tiers"}

**Scenario**: An LLM API platform serves Enterprise, Professional, and Free service tiers across shared and dedicated hardware.

**Diagnosis**: Unpartitioned multi-tenant pools allow Free-tier traffic spikes or malformed requests to degrade Enterprise SLOs. Bulkheads place Enterprise on dedicated GPU pools (99.9 percent availability), allocate 70 percent capacity to Professional, and cap Free tier at 30 percent best-effort capacity.

**Systems lesson**: Bulkheads concentrate isolation overhead where business requirements dictate. Hardware partitioning reduces cross-tenant compute and memory contention. SLO compliance still depends on sufficient capacity, admission policy, shared dependencies, and failure handling.

:::

Multi-tenant isolation limits the blast radius of excess demand, but it does not create capacity. Once protected queues approach their latency budgets, the service needs a control loop that can add replicas before admission begins to fail.

## Autoscaling and Capacity Control {#sec-inference-scale-autoscaling-capacity-control}

A serving autoscaler\index{Autoscaling!capacity control} that reacts only to average accelerator utilization can scale in the wrong direction. Decode can saturate memory bandwidth while arithmetic units appear idle, long prompts can consume prefill capacity before request count rises, and queued work can violate an SLO while fleet-wide utilization remains moderate. The control signal must represent outstanding work relative to phase-specific service capacity. Every replica the controller adds is also a claim on accelerators that training jobs may hold, so the fleet-level arbitration of @sec-fleet-orchestration-serving bounds how quickly and how far serving can grow.

For a conventional fixed-cost model, queueing delay and request rate per ready replica can be sufficient. Autoregressive serving needs at least separate prompt-token and output-token arrival rates, active KV-cache occupancy, and the observed service rates of the prefill and decode pools. The controller converts each signal into a required replica count, then takes the maximum requirement plus failure and forecast headroom. Scaling on SLO goodput prevents the controller from counting requests that complete after their TTFT or TPOT targets as usable capacity. For the same reason, a threshold set as a fraction of the P99 target adapts automatically when a new model version runs slower, whereas a utilization target must be retuned by hand. The controller acts by changing the replica count; resizing an accelerator allocation in place requires restarting the process and reloading its weights, so vertical scaling helps mainly the CPU stages around the model.

Scale-up and scale-down require asymmetric evidence. Scale-up acts on sustained queue growth, forecast demand, or declining deadline slack because cold-start delay makes late reactions expensive. Scale-down requires low demand over a longer window, enough spare capacity to survive one replica failure, and a drain plan for in-flight requests and any optional session cache. This hysteresis\index{Autoscaling!hysteresis} prevents oscillation in which replicas repeatedly load large weights, accept work, and terminate before amortizing startup cost.

The controller also needs observability that distinguishes demand from impaired supply. Request rate, input and output tokens, queue age, TTFT, TPOT, deadline misses, admission rejections, ready replicas, model-load failures, and per-phase service rate form the minimum feedback set. Without replica readiness and service-rate measurements, an autoscaler can respond to a sick replica by adding cold replicas indefinitely while the original failure remains hidden.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: cold-start-timeline
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COLD START AND PREDICTIVE SCALING (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: cold-start and predictive-scaling examples in
# │          @sec-inference-scale-autoscaling-capacity-control.
# │
# │ Goal: Derive the replica cold-start time from artifact size and storage
# │       bandwidth, and the GPU spend recovered by predictive scaling.
# │ Show: ~4.7 min artifact fetch, ~6.7 min cold start, 45 vs 30 peak
# │       replicas, 33 percent saving.
# │ How: T_cold = T_provision + artifact / storage_bw + T_load_warmup.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_percent, fmt_time

class ColdStartTimeline:
    """Cold-start decomposition and predictive-scaling saving."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    artifact = Models.Language.Llama2_70B.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    storage_bw = 0.5 * (GB / second)  # scenario assumption: effective object-storage read rate
    t_provision = 60 * second  # scenario assumption: instance acquisition and boot
    t_load_warmup = 60 * second  # scenario assumption: device load and warmup
    reactive_peak_replicas = 45  # scenario assumption: reactive-only peak fleet
    predictive_peak_replicas = 30  # scenario assumption: forecast peak fleet (schedule table)
    lead_min = 30  # scenario assumption: pre-warm lead before each ramp

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    t_fetch = (artifact / storage_bw).to(second)
    t_cold = t_provision + t_fetch + t_load_warmup
    spend_saving = 1 - predictive_peak_replicas / reactive_peak_replicas

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(t_fetch > t_provision + t_load_warmup, "Artifact fetch should dominate the cold start")
    check(t_cold.to("minute").magnitude < lead_min, "Pre-warm lead must exceed the cold start")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    fetch_min_str = fmt_time(t_fetch, 'minute', precision=1, commas=False, style='word')
    provision_min_str = fmt_time(t_provision, 'minute', precision=0, commas=False, style='word')
    load_warmup_min_str = fmt_time(t_load_warmup, 'minute', precision=0, commas=False, style='word')
    cold_min_str = fmt_time(t_cold, 'minute', precision=1, commas=False, style='word')
    cold_min_attr_str = fmt_time(round(t_cold.to('minute').magnitude), 'minute', precision=0, commas=False, style='word', attributive=True)
    storage_bw_str = fmt_bandwidth(storage_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=1, commas=False)
    reactive_peak_str = fmt_int(reactive_peak_replicas, commas=False)
    predictive_peak_str = fmt_int(predictive_peak_replicas, commas=False)
    spend_saving_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(spend_saving, 2), precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
    lead_min_str = fmt_time(lead_min, 'minute', precision=0, commas=False, style='word')
```

::: {#exmp-inference-cold-start-timeline-llama-70b .callout-example title="Cold start timeline for Llama-70B"}

**Scenario**: An autoscaling engine provisions a new Llama-70B serving replica on an H100 GPU instance during a sudden traffic surge.

**Diagnosis**: Bringing up a fresh replica takes about `{python} ColdStartTimeline.cold_min_str` ($T_{\text{cold start}} = T_{\text{provision}} + T_{\text{load}} + T_{\text{warmup}}$)\index{Cold start!LLM replica loading}: `{python} ColdStartTimeline.provision_min_str` to acquire and boot the instance, `{python} ColdStartTimeline.fetch_min_str` to fetch `{python} InferenceSetup.llama70b_fp16_gb_str` of model artifacts from object storage at an effective `{python} ColdStartTimeline.storage_bw_str`, and `{python} ColdStartTimeline.load_warmup_min_str` for device loading and warmup. Reactive autoscaling cannot absorb the surge before requests time out.

**Systems lesson**: Cold-start latency depends on artifact size, effective storage bandwidth, provisioning delay, compilation, and warmup. The controller must measure this distribution and begin provisioning far enough ahead that its high percentile fits inside the forecast horizon.

:::

::: {#exmp-inference-predictive-scaling-traffic .callout-example title="Predictive scaling for traffic"}

**Scenario**: A commercial chatbot service faces predictable diurnal traffic patterns, ramping from 500 QPS at night to 3,000 QPS at peak.

**Diagnosis**: Reactive scaling triggers scale-ups only after traffic arrives, so each morning ramp (06:00 and 09:00 UTC) overloads the fleet for the `{python} ColdStartTimeline.cold_min_attr_str` cold start of every new replica.

**Systems lesson**: Predictive autoscaling\index{Autoscaling!predictive scaling} converts diurnal time-series forecasts into scheduled pre-warming windows, as shown in the schedule breakdown (@tbl-inference-chatbot-predictive-schedule). Triggering scale-up actions `{python} ColdStartTimeline.lead_min_str` before expected ramps leaves replicas fully warmed when traffic arrives.

| **Time** |  **Action**  | **Replicas Active** | **Replicas Starting** |
|:---------|:------------:|:-------------------:|:---------------------:|
| 05:30    |   Scale up   |          5          |      +10 warming      |
| 06:00    | Traffic ramp |          15         |           -           |
| 08:30    |   Scale up   |          15         |      +15 warming      |
| 09:00    | Peak traffic |          30         |           -           |
| 17:00    |  Scale down  |          20         |    -10 terminating    |
| 20:00    |  Scale down  |          10         |    -10 terminating    |
| 00:00    |  Scale down  |          5          |     -5 terminating    |

: **Predictive scaling schedule**: Per-time-bucket scaling actions, active replicas, and replicas in cold-start warming for the chatbot workload. {#tbl-inference-chatbot-predictive-schedule}

**Systems insight**: A reactive-only autoscaler must over-provision during each ramp (about `{python} ColdStartTimeline.reactive_peak_str` replicas at peak in this scenario) because it cannot anticipate the curve. Predictive scaling sizes the fleet to the forecast peak (`{python} ColdStartTimeline.predictive_peak_str` replicas), recovering roughly `{python} ColdStartTimeline.spend_saving_pct_str` of peak GPU spend without sacrificing latency headroom.

:::

The cost savings demonstrated in example \ref{exmp-inference-predictive-scaling-traffic} depend on anticipating traffic before it arrives. As plotted in @fig-predictive-reactive-scaling, proactive provisioning avoids the SLO violations that reactive-only systems suffer during ramp-up periods.

::: {#fig-predictive-reactive-scaling fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Predictive vs. reactive scaling**: Reactive scaling (red line) responds to traffic spikes after they occur, leading to periods of under-provisioning where SLOs are violated due to cold start latency. Predictive scaling (blue line) anticipates traffic and begins provisioning capacity before the spike arrives, ensuring consistent performance." fig-alt="Time-series plot with traffic curve, reactive capacity lagging behind the spike, and predictive capacity scaling ahead of it."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style
import numpy as np

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(8.5, 4.6))

c_dark = COLORS['primary']
c_blue = COLORS['BlueLine']
c_red = COLORS['RedLine']
c_border = '#CBD5E1'

t = np.linspace(0, 9.5, 500)
traffic = 1.0 + 3.0 * np.exp(-((t - 5.0) ** 2) / (2 * 0.95**2))

# Reactive capacity: lags until spike peak approaches at t=5.1, ramps to 4.2 by t=5.7
reactive = np.piecewise(
    t,
    [t < 5.1, (t >= 5.1) & (t <= 5.7), t > 5.7],
    [1.2, lambda t: 1.2 + (4.2 - 1.2) * ((t - 5.1) / 0.6), 4.2],
)

# Predictive capacity: anticipates spike, ramps from t=3.2 to t=4.3
predictive = np.piecewise(
    t,
    [t < 3.2, (t >= 3.2) & (t <= 4.3), t > 4.3],
    [1.2, lambda t: 1.2 + (4.2 - 1.2) * ((t - 3.2) / 1.1), 4.2],
)

# Curves
ax.plot(
    t,
    traffic,
    color=c_dark,
    linestyle='--',
    linewidth=2.0,
    label='Actual Traffic Demand',
    zorder=4,
)
ax.plot(
    t,
    predictive,
    color=c_blue,
    linewidth=2.2,
    label='Predictive Capacity (Proactive)',
    zorder=5,
)
ax.plot(
    t,
    reactive,
    color=c_red,
    linewidth=2.2,
    label='Reactive Capacity (Lagging)',
    zorder=5,
)

# Shaded deficit (SLO violation)
slo_mask = traffic > reactive
ax.fill_between(
    t,
    reactive,
    traffic,
    where=slo_mask,
    color=COLORS['RedFill'],
    edgecolor=c_red,
    hatch='///',
    alpha=0.4,
    label='SLO Violation Deficit (Under-provisioned)',
    zorder=2,
)

# Shaded proactive safety buffer
headroom_mask = (predictive > traffic) & (t >= 3.2) & (t <= 6.8)
ax.fill_between(
    t,
    traffic,
    predictive,
    where=headroom_mask,
    color=COLORS['BlueFill'],
    alpha=0.35,
    zorder=1,
)

# Annotations with clean arrow placements
ax.annotate(
    'SLO VIOLATION DEFICIT\n(Cold-start latency & dropped requests)',
    xy=(4.4, 2.8),
    xytext=(2.2, 3.6),
    fontsize=8.0,
    fontweight='bold',
    color=c_red,
    ha='center',
    bbox=dict(
        boxstyle='round,pad=0.3',
        facecolor='white',
        edgecolor=c_red,
        lw=0.9,
    ),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=c_red, lw=1.0),
)

ax.annotate(
    'Predictive Scale-Up\n(Capacity ready on-time)',
    xy=(3.5, 1.8),
    xytext=(1.8, 2.0),
    fontsize=8.0,
    fontweight='bold',
    color=c_blue,
    ha='center',
    bbox=dict(
        boxstyle='round,pad=0.3',
        facecolor='white',
        edgecolor=c_blue,
        lw=0.9,
    ),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=c_blue, lw=1.0),
)

ax.annotate(
    'Reactive Detection Lag\n(Late scale-up after traffic onset)',
    xy=(5.3, 2.4),
    xytext=(7.4, 2.2),
    fontsize=8.0,
    fontweight='bold',
    color=c_red,
    ha='center',
    bbox=dict(
        boxstyle='round,pad=0.3',
        facecolor='white',
        edgecolor=c_red,
        lw=0.9,
    ),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=c_red, lw=1.0),
)

ax.set_xlim(0, 9.5)
ax.set_ylim(0, 4.8)
ax.set_xlabel('Time (Arbitrary Units / Minutes)')
ax.set_ylabel('Load / Serving Capacity (Normalized)')

ax.legend(
    loc='upper right',
    frameon=True,
    facecolor='white',
    edgecolor=c_border,
    framealpha=0.95,
    fontsize=8.0,
)

plt.tight_layout()
```

:::

### Warm pool management {#sec-inference-scale-warm-pool-management-a360}

Maintaining a pool of prewarmed replicas reduces effective cold-start time by buying idle readiness before demand arrives. Warm pool\index{Warm pool!replica management} sizing starts from the demand the pool must absorb before new capacity can be provisioned: the expected spike divided by per-replica throughput, multiplied by a headroom factor for forecast error. A service that expects a spike to double its demand and applies a headroom factor of 1.5 needs ready capacity, hot and warm together, of three times its baseline replica count. The cost of that readiness is $\text{Pool size} \times \text{GPU cost/hour} \times \text{Idle fraction}$, a direct trade between response speed and idle-capacity expense. Tiered warm pools, summarized in @tbl-warm-pool-tiers, soften the trade by holding replicas at different readiness levels, each with its own activation delay and cost:

| **Tier** | **State**                                   | **Activation requirement**           | **Cost while waiting**              |
|:---------|:--------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------|:------------------------------------|
| **Hot**  | Model running on allocated GPU              | Route admitted work                  | Allocated GPU and service resources |
| **Warm** | Capacity allocated; runtime partly prepared | Finish initialization and validation | Allocated resources remain billable |
| **Cold** | GPU not allocated                           | Acquire capacity, load, and warm up  | Artifact storage; no allocated GPU  |

: **Tiered warm pool readiness levels**: Readiness trades activation delay against idle resource cost. Actual delay and billing depend on the deployment. Cold capacity is subject to quotas and physical availability. {#tbl-warm-pool-tiers}

When a traffic spike hits, the controller routes work to ready replicas, activates prepared capacity, and requests additional instances if needed. Pool sizing must cover the measured provisioning delay and include an overload policy for capacity that cannot be acquired in time.

### Scaling response time analysis {#sec-inference-scale-scaling-response-time-analysis-0dbf}

The scaling response budget is the sum of the control loop's detection, decision, provisioning, and warmup delays. @Eq-scaling-response makes those phases explicit:

$$T_{\text{response}} = T_{\text{detect}} + T_{\text{decide}} + T_{\text{provision}} + T_{\text{warmup}}$$ {#eq-scaling-response}

@Tbl-scaling-response-components decomposes each term and identifies its primary optimization path:

| **Component**    | **Duration** |     **Optimization**    |
|:-----------------|:------------:|:-----------------------:|
| **Detection**    |   10--60s    | Reduce metrics interval |
| **Decision**     |    1--5s     |    Faster autoscaler    |
| **Provisioning** |  30s--5min   |        Warm pools       |
| **Warmup**       |    5--30s    |      Precompilation     |

: **Scaling response time components**: The four phases of a scaling event with typical durations and their primary optimization lever. Provisioning dominates the budget by an order of magnitude, which is why warm pools are a high-leverage optimization for latency-sensitive serving fleets. {#tbl-scaling-response-components}

Provisioning dominates this budget, so warm pools, which remove provisioning for anticipated demand, are the highest-leverage optimization. The remaining terms shrink with finer-grained metrics, at the cost of noisier signals, with scaling plans precomputed for predicted scenarios, and with precompiled inference engines that skip just-in-time (JIT) compilation during warmup.

### Spot and preemptible instances {#sec-inference-scale-spot-preemptible-instances-c969}

Discounted interruptible capacity[^fn-spot-instance-inference] enters serving through the same purchasing tiers that fleet capacity planning uses (@tbl-cloud-capacity-reservation-tiers): reserved capacity for the steady baseline, on-demand capacity for bursts, and spot capacity for work that tolerates revocation. None of these tiers makes a replica immune to failure, so the serving question is whether a revoked replica can drain, reroute, or recompute its requests without violating their SLO. The provider's warning window is the binding constraint.

[^fn-spot-instance-inference]: **Spot-instance economics**\index{Spot Instance Economics}\index{Spot Instances!inference}: @eq-fleet-orchestration-spot-cost in @sec-fleet-orchestration-spot-instances derives the effective cost of preemptible capacity from its productive fraction. For inference, revocation can also destroy in-flight requests and KV-cache state, so the productive fraction must be charged for draining, rerouting, and restoring capacity.

Spot termination handling is a race against the provider's warning window. @Lst-spot-termination orders the shutdown path so new work stops first, in-flight work drains while time remains, recoverable state is persisted, and the load balancer stops sending traffic before the instance disappears.

::: {#lst-spot-termination lst-cap="**Spot Termination Handling**: Graceful shutdown sequence that stops admission, deregisters from the load balancer, drains in-flight requests, and persists recoverable state."}

```{.python}
async def handle_spot_termination():
    # Received 2-minute warning
    # 1. Stop admission and remove the replica from routing
    stop_accepting_requests()
    deregister_from_loadbalancer()

    # 2. Complete in-flight requests (if possible)
    await complete_inflight(timeout=90)

    # 3. Save state for resumption elsewhere
    save_kv_cache_to_storage()

    # 4. Terminate gracefully
    shutdown()
```

:::

The gateway architecture diagrammed in @fig-spot-aware-routing partitions incoming traffic between on-demand and spot pools according to declared SLO class: latency-critical requests route unconditionally to reserved instances, while best-effort traffic absorbs preemption risks on discounted spot capacity.

::: {#fig-spot-aware-routing fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Spot-aware traffic distribution**: The gateway classifies requests by SLO and routes 70 percent of traffic, the SLO-critical share, to on-demand replicas that face no spot reclamation, and 30 percent, the best-effort share, to discounted spot replicas that can be preempted. When a spot worker receives an eviction notice, the gateway stops routing to it while it drains, and best-effort requests tolerate occasional retries. The traffic split is illustrative; cost savings depend on provisioned capacity, discounts, retries, and idle headroom." fig-alt="A Requests box, tagged with an SLO class, feeds a violet Spot-aware gateway box that classifies SLO, watches preemption, and drains. A solid arrow labeled SLO-critical (70%) leads to an On-demand pool with three reserved workers, 0 to 2. A dashed arrow labeled best-effort (30%) leads to a dashed Spot pool with spot workers 3 and 4 and a red dashed Worker 5 marked draining. A red dashed arrow labeled eviction notice runs from Worker 5 back to the gateway."}

:::

Savings under this split depend on provisioned GPU-hours, discounts, retries, and reserve capacity rather than on the traffic share, and spot capacity changes none of the fault-tolerance requirements of the SLO-critical path.

### Global inference infrastructure {#sec-inference-scale-global-inference-infrastructure-df52}

Extending resource isolation and failure boundaries beyond a single data center leads to global infrastructure. Global serving becomes necessary when distance, failure domains, or data-residency constraints exceed what one region can hide. A user in Tokyo expects low-latency responses regardless of where models were trained or where the company headquarters is located; the engineering choice is whether to replicate computation, cache repeated work, or centralize the model and pay the network penalty. The architectural patterns are useful only when tied to that choice. @Fig-serving-deployment-stack shows the tiers a global request crosses before it reaches a model replica, each with its own share of the latency budget.

::: {#fig-serving-deployment-stack fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Serving deployment stack**: A global request crosses three tiers before reaching a model replica. Tier 1 edge points of presence (PoPs) answer repeated requests from cache; a miss passes to Tier 2, where the gateway applies rate limits and authentication and the router picks a destination; Tier 3 GPU workers run prefill and decode while an autoscaler sizes the fleet from queue depth and KV cache use. Tokens stream back up the same path. The per-tier latency budgets on the right are illustrative." fig-alt="Three stacked tiers. Tier 1, edge cache: three Edge PoP cards labeled cached responses. Tier 2, gateway and router: rate limiter, auth, model router and telemetry cards. Tier 3, model serving cluster: three GPU workers, each with prefill and decode boxes, plus an autoscaler card driven by queue depth and KV use. Down arrows labeled cache miss and dispatch and up arrows labeled streamed response and token stream join the tiers. A right column gives illustrative latency budgets of under 10 ms, under 50 ms and under 2 s."}

#### Drivers for multi-region deployment {#sec-inference-scale-multiregion-matters-d7d3}

Single-region deployment creates three fundamental limitations. The most immediate is the latency floor imposed by network round-trip time (RTT) to distant users, quantified in @tbl-rtt-by-user-location:

| **User Location** | **RTT to US-East** | **RTT to Local Region** |
|:------------------|:------------------:|:-----------------------:|
| **New York**      |       10 ms        |          10 ms          |
| **London**        |       75 ms        |          10 ms          |
| **Tokyo**         |       150 ms       |          10 ms          |
| **Sydney**        |       200 ms       |          10 ms          |

: **Network RTT by user location**: A single US-East deployment imposes a 75 to 200 ms RTT on European, Asian, and Australian users, an order of magnitude above the local-region floor. For interactive workloads where each request makes several model calls, this latency floor compounds quickly, motivating multi-region deployment for any globally distributed user base. {#tbl-rtt-by-user-location tbl-colwidths="[34,33,33]"}

For interactive applications (chatbots, autocomplete), these delays compound across multiple model calls per request. Beyond latency, single-region deployment creates a single point of failure: cloud region outages, while rare, affect all users simultaneously. Regulatory constraints add a third dimension, as data residency requirements (the General Data Protection Regulation and data sovereignty laws) may require processing user data within specific geographic boundaries. The resulting patterns form a decision ladder: regional replicas pay the highest deployment cost but minimize RTT and isolate regional failures; edge caching pays operational complexity only when queries repeat; and cross-region sharding is a last resort for capacity shortages because inter-region latency overwhelms per-stage compute.

#### Global load balancing with regional replicas {#sec-inference-scale-pattern-1-global-load-balancing-regional-replicas-b7ac}

In the multi-region topology diagrammed in @fig-global-inference-multiregion, a global load balancer\index{Global load balancing!regional replicas} routes user traffic to the nearest geographic cluster based on measured round-trip latency, while a centralized registry synchronizes versioned model weights across independent regional replicas.

::: {#fig-global-inference-multiregion fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Global load balancing across inference regions**: A global load balancer routes each user to the nearest healthy region (@tbl-rtt-by-user-location gives the round-trip times this avoids). Each region (US-East, EU-West, Asia-Pacific) runs independent replicas of the same model, and EU requests can stay in the EU to meet data-residency rules. A shared model registry supplies versioned weights to every region. If a region fails, the load balancer reroutes its users to the next nearest healthy region." fig-alt="A Global load balancer box at the top fans out through a bus to three region frames, US-East, EU-West, and Asia-Pacific. Each frame has a one-line role, such as EU data stays in region, and two replica boxes labeled Replica 0 and Replica 1, GPU server. Below, a wide Model registry box, versioned weights for every region, sends dashed green sync arrows up to each region."}

:::

Independent regional replicas reduce RTT from 150--200 ms to under 10 ms for distant users, while the shared model registry provides a common source of versioned artifacts. Model synchronization is the first architectural concern, because updates must propagate to all regions. Push-based synchronization sends artifacts to each region, while pull-based synchronization lets regions fetch them after notification or polling. Neither mechanism alone guarantees consistent serving versions. Artifact verification, readiness gates, and coordinated activation determine when a region may serve the new version; hybrid synchronization combines push notification with pull verification.

Version consistency is the second concern. During rollouts, different regions may briefly serve different versions. For most applications this is acceptable, but applications requiring strict consistency need version pinning in request routing. Rollouts therefore proceed region by region. A canary deployment\index{Canary deployment!global rollout} first sends a small share of one region's traffic, often around 1 percent, to the new version and holds it long enough to collect the observations its release gate requires. A few hours is a reasonable starting point; @sec-ml-operations-scale-canary-deployment-3d8b sizes the holding time from the required sample count and the canary's traffic share (@eq-canary-duration). Each later expansion is itself a gate: no region adopts the new version until the previous region has held its error-rate, latency, and quality targets for a full monitoring window, and rollback returns a region to the prior version while preserving the new one for debugging.

#### Edge caching with central inference {#sec-inference-scale-pattern-2-edge-caching-central-inference-f08e}

For models too large to replicate globally, caching responses at the edge\index{Edge caching!central inference} eliminates redundant inference for repeated queries. @Fig-edge-cache-routing shows the two paths: a cache hit returns in under 10 ms from the nearest edge node; a cache miss traverses the full backend and populates the cache on return.

::: {#fig-edge-cache-routing fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Cache hit and cache miss paths at the edge**: A query first reaches the nearest edge point of presence (PoP). On a cache hit, the edge returns the stored response in under 10 ms without touching a GPU. On a miss, the request passes through the regional gateway to the central GPU cluster, which runs prefill and decode. Generated tokens stream back to the user, and the response is stored at the edge for later queries. Hit rate determines the saving; open-ended generative workloads repeat rarely and gain little from this pattern." fig-alt="Four boxes in a row joined by arrows: User, Edge PoP response cache, Regional gateway for auth and rate limiting, and GPU cluster for prefill and decode. The arrows are labeled query, miss, and forward. A green path above the row returns from the Edge PoP to the User, labeled cache hit, returned from edge in under 10 ms. A navy path below the row returns from the GPU cluster to the User, labeled cache miss, generated tokens stream back. A dashed green branch from that path goes up into the Edge PoP, labeled store response."}

:::

The two paths in @fig-edge-cache-routing highlight the latency difference: cache hits avoid the backend round-trip, while misses incur it. Effectiveness depends on request repeatability across workloads such as autocomplete, FAQ chatbots, open-ended chat, and code generation. @Tbl-edge-cache-hit-rates supplies illustrative hit-rate envelopes for sensitivity analysis; an actual design must derive hit rate and correctness from production traces.

| **Workload**        | **Cache Hit Rate** | **Suitability** |
|:--------------------|:------------------:|:---------------:|
| **Autocomplete**    |      60--80%       |    Excellent    |
| **FAQ chatbot**     |      40--60%       |       Good      |
| **Open-ended chat** |       5--15%       |       Poor      |
| **Code generation** |      20--40%       |     Moderate    |

: **Illustrative edge-cache hit-rate envelopes**: Assumed cache-hit ranges for four workload shapes. These values are scenario inputs, not universal workload statistics. Trace-derived repeatability, response validity, and latency saved determine whether caching is worthwhile. {#tbl-edge-cache-hit-rates}

Semantic caching[^fn-semantic-cache-tradeoff] (caching based on embedding similarity rather than exact match) can improve hit rates for open-ended workloads.

[^fn-semantic-cache-tradeoff]: [offset=-10mm] **Semantic caching**\index{Semantic Caching!trade-off}: A similarity lookup can reuse responses beyond exact string matches, but it adds retrieval work and can return an invalid answer when superficially similar queries require different responses. The similarity threshold therefore trades cache coverage against correctness.

#### Cross-region model sharding {#sec-inference-scale-pattern-3-cross-region-model-sharding-7a2f}

Cross-region model sharding is a last-resort capacity strategy rather than a normal latency optimization. For the largest models, pipeline parallelism can theoretically span regions: a router assigns early layers to one region and later layers to another. This pattern is rarely practical because inter-region network latency (75–150 ms) dominates compute time per stage (1–5 ms), making cross-region pipeline parallelism 10--100$\times$ slower than co-located deployment. It applies only when no single region has sufficient GPU capacity for the full model.

Because cross-region sharding is so costly on the steady-state path, most production designs keep inference co-located and use other regions for resilience. The cross-region question therefore shifts from splitting one request across regions to deciding how quickly traffic can move when a region fails.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\newpage
:::

#### Cross-region failover {#sec-inference-scale-crossregion-failover-0d67}

When a region becomes unavailable, traffic must reroute to healthy regions. @Lst-active-failover shows active-active failover routing logic that falls back to the next healthy region after timeout or unavailability.

::: {#lst-active-failover lst-cap="**Active-Active Failover**: Global routing implementation that attempts the primary regional endpoint with a strict timeout before falling back to the secondary healthy region." lst-pos="H"}

```{.python}
# Simplified global routing logic
def route_request(user_region, request):
    primary = get_nearest_healthy_region(user_region)
    secondary = get_second_nearest_healthy_region(user_region)

    try:
        return call_region(primary, request, timeout=2.0)
    except (Timeout, RegionUnavailable):
        # Failover with increased latency
        return call_region(secondary, request, timeout=5.0)
```

:::

Rerouting is the simpler half of regional failover. For stateful LLM serving, the receiving region must also rebuild lost session state, regenerating KV caches from retained conversation history, and it must have the headroom to absorb the failed region's load. @Sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-session-affinity-stateful-failover-27b2 covers the state recovery, and @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability-reliability-replication-strategies-aaa2 covers the regional headroom and the gradual return of traffic that keeps a recovered region from failing over again.

#### Cost optimization across regions {#sec-inference-scale-cost-optimization-across-regions-c1c2}

GPU pricing varies by provider, contract, region, and time. @Tbl-gpu-region-pricing uses a hypothetical price snapshot to show how placement can balance cost against latency requirements; it must not be used for procurement:

| **Region**  | **H100 Spot Price** | **On-Demand** | **Latency to US Users** |
|:------------|:-------------------:|:-------------:|:-----------------------:|
| **US-East** |      \$2.50/hr      |   \$4.00/hr   |        10--50 ms        |
| **US-West** |      \$2.30/hr      |   \$3.80/hr   |        30--70 ms        |
| **EU-West** |      \$2.80/hr      |   \$4.20/hr   |        75--100 ms       |

: **Hypothetical regional price and latency snapshot**: Scenario prices and RTTs illustrate a placement calculation. Both inputs are time- and provider-specific; a deployment must refresh them from its contract and measured network paths before making a routing decision. {#tbl-gpu-region-pricing}

Cost-aware routing directs latency-tolerant workloads (batch inference, background processing) to the cheapest available region (@lst-cost-aware-routing).

::: {#lst-cost-aware-routing lst-cap="**Cost-Aware Routing**: Priority-based request router that dispatches low-priority batch requests to the lowest-cost region with available capacity while routing latency-sensitive interactive traffic to the nearest region."}

```{.python}
def route_batch_request(request):
    if request.priority == "low":
        # Route to cheapest region with capacity
        return get_cheapest_region_with_capacity()
    else:
        # Route to nearest region
        return get_nearest_region(request.user_location)
```

:::

Time-of-day routing can reduce batch cost when regional price differences exceed data-transfer and coordination costs. Savings require a workload-specific calculation, and interactive traffic must retain its own latency budget.

Regional placement completes the serving hierarchy, from one request's batch slot to a fleet that spans continents. The design cases that follow show how these techniques combine when a service must meet specific cost and latency targets.

## Case Studies {#sec-inference-scale-case-studies-9689}

These four design cases are illustrative composites rather than descriptions of named companies' internal deployments, and their request rates, latency budgets, hardware allocations, and update cadences follow the chapter's scenario convention. Each case binds on a different constraint: embedding scale, variable-length generation, cascade cost, or multimodal freshness. Orca and vLLM supply the previously cited scheduling and memory-management mechanisms; the scenarios combine those ideas with routing, sharding, and admission control.

### Embedding-heavy recommendation serving {#sec-inference-scale-meta-recommendation-serving-bede}

An embedding-heavy recommendation service\index{Recommendation system!embedding-heavy serving case} binds on sparse lookup rather than dense forward-pass compute. This scenario models feeds, advertising, and content ranking with a large distributed embedding store.

The operational scale explains why embedding locality dominates the architecture: the service processes billions of requests per day under a P99 budget below $10\text{ ms}$ for the ranking service, nested inside the roughly `{python} ArchetypeBTailAtScale.p99_slo_ms_str` end-to-end tail target of Archetype B (DLRM at Scale), spanning hundreds of distinct model variants over an entity catalog comprising trillions of unique sparse features.

The serving stack separates sparse lookup from dense ranking:

```
User request → Feature collection → Embedding lookup → Model inference → Response

                    |                     |                  |
                    v                     v                  v
             Feature Store        Embedding Servers      GPU Inference
             (CPU, DRAM)         (CPU + SSD, 1000s)     (GPU, 100s)
```

The hybrid sharding strategy\index{Embedding table!hybrid sharding} in lighthouse \ref{lhs-inference-embedding-sharding-at-meta} supplies the sparse path: replication protects hot entries, column sharding spreads warm-entry access, and row sharding places the cold tail. Feature-level batching then combines lookups across requests. The remaining design decision is where each stage runs. In the GPU-CPU hybrid architecture\index{Hardware specialization!GPU-CPU hybrid}, memory-rich CPU servers serve sparse embeddings while GPUs execute dense ranking. @Tbl-meta-dlrm-hybrid-hardware connects that placement to the end-to-end latency budget.

| **Component**          | **Hardware** | **Latency** | **Throughput** |
|:-----------------------|:------------:|:-----------:|:--------------:|
| **Embedding lookup**   |  CPU + SSD   |     2 ms    | 50M lookups/s  |
| **Feature processing** |     CPU      |     1 ms    |   10M ops/s    |
| **Dense ranking**      |     GPU      |    1.5 ms   |  100K infs/s   |

: **Illustrative hybrid CPU/GPU architecture**: Illustrative hardware-workload mapping for the recommendation scenario. CPU + SSD handles the bandwidth-bound sparse path; CPU handles low-arithmetic-intensity feature processing; GPU handles the compute-dense ranking forward pass. The component budgets exclude queueing and response delivery; their sum alone does not establish the P99 target. {#tbl-meta-dlrm-hybrid-hardware tbl-colwidths="[32,22,16,30]"}

The serving lesson is that recommendation latency is often dominated by embedding lookup rather than dense model inference. Feature-parallel batching and a hybrid CPU-GPU architecture match the hardware to the sparse and dense halves of the workload, which sets up a contrast with GPT-style API serving where request variance and autoregressive state dominate.

### A multi-model generation API {#sec-inference-scale-openai-api-infrastructure-a65e}

A multi-model generation API\index{Generation API!serving case} binds on request variance: short prompts, long-context requests, and different model sizes share capacity while users expect predictable TTFT. The infrastructure serves GPT-class models to large developer and application workloads while maintaining quality of service across diverse workloads.

The operating scale explains why continuous batching and admission control dominate the infrastructure: the platform serves millions of requests per hour under a time-to-first-token target below $2\text{ s}$, hosting models that range from billions to hundreds of billions of parameters with context lengths reaching up to 128K tokens.

The serving stack separates routing, scheduling, cache management, and shard groups:

```
API Gateway → Rate Limiting → Request Router → Model Cluster → Response Streaming

                                     |
                                     v
                              +-------------+
                              | Model Pool  |
                              | +---------+ |
                              | | Large   | |
                              | | 8×H100  | |
                              | +---------+ |
                              | +---------+ |
                              | | Smaller | |
                              | | 4×A100  | |
                              | +---------+ |
                              +-------------+
```

The main design decision is to prevent long prompts from blocking decode service for everyone else.

An Orca-style design uses continuous batching to refill completed slots. Chunked prefill limits interference from long prompts by interleaving prompt chunks with ongoing generation. The TTFT target must be validated across prompt lengths; admitting a 128K-token prompt does not imply that it meets the short-request latency target. @Tbl-batching-strategies-comparison contrasts the three approaches:

| **Batching Strategy**    | **Slot reuse**                  | **Long-prompt interference**                                            |
|:-------------------------|:--------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Static batching**      | Waits for batch completion      | Monolithic prefill can delay decode                                     |
| **Continuous batching**  | Refills at iteration boundaries | Monolithic prefill can still delay decode                               |
| **Continuous + chunked** | Refills at iteration boundaries | Limits prefill work per iteration; tail latency still needs measurement |

: **Batching strategy comparison**: Slot reuse and prefill interference are separate concerns. Continuous batching addresses the first; chunking gives control over the second. Neither mechanism alone establishes utilization or latency numbers. {#tbl-batching-strategies-comparison}

Large GPT-class models often require 8-way or greater tensor parallelism for memory capacity and latency. A representative deployment allocates eight H100 GPUs per large-model shard group connected via high-speed NVLink for intra-node communication, with consistent hashing at the gateway to maintain session affinity and enable cross-turn KV cache reuse.

To prevent noisy neighbors from exhausting capacity, the illustrative API applies hierarchical rate limiting across multiple granularities: per-API-key request arrival limits, per-API-key token-per-minute consumption limits, organization-level capacity quotas, and global model capacity ceilings.

A possible capacity policy shifts resources between models based on queue depth, subject to model-loading delay and each service's minimum allocation:

```
if large_model_queue_depth > threshold:
    # Migrate some smaller-model capacity to the larger model
    reallocate_cluster_capacity(from="smaller-model", to="large-model", fraction=0.2)
```

LLM APIs are governed by variance control. Continuous batching, prefix caching, and multi-tier rate limiting keep long prompts, repeated conversational context, and traffic spikes from turning one user's request into everyone else's latency. Search ranking faces a different shape of the same problem. Many cheaper models must cooperate under one strict deadline.

### Search ranking under a deadline {#sec-inference-scale-google-search-ranking-aab2}

The search-ranking scenario\index{Search ranking!illustrative cascade} binds on cascade cost: each query coordinates many smaller models under one end-to-end latency budget rather than serving one large model. The ensemble combines specialized models for query understanding, document relevance, and result ranking.

The operational scale explains why a cascade architecture is mandatory: the system must process billions of searches per day under a strict end-to-end latency target of less than $200\text{ ms}$, evaluating thousands of candidate documents per query across dozens of specialized models.

To meet this latency budget while evaluating thousands of documents, the system employs a ranking cascade\index{Ranking cascade!multi-stage filtering} shown in @fig-ranking-cascade that progressively narrows the candidate set through increasingly expensive models.

::: {#fig-ranking-cascade fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Ranking cascade architecture**: To optimize latency and cost, search and recommendation systems use a cascade of increasingly complex models. Early stages (Retrieval) filter millions of candidates down to thousands using fast, cheap heuristics. Later stages use expensive, high-precision models only on the most promising candidates." fig-alt="Funnel diagram with four stages narrowing from retrieval of one million items to final ranking of ten items."}
